statedGuarantee: Every MCP tool call, A2A task delegation and generic HTTP call carries an Invocation-Bound Capability Token (IBCT): an Ed25519-signed, append-only chain (compact mode = signed JWT for single-hop; chained mode = Biscuit + Datalog for multi-hop) that fuses identity, holder-side attenuated authorization and provenance. Claimed properties: any verifier can establish offline (no authorization-server round trip) who authorized an action, through which agents it flowed, and what constraints applied at each hop; a delegatee may only narrow, never widen, scope/budget/expiry; delegation depth is bounded by max_depth declared in Block 0; every delegation block must carry a non-empty context string for audit integrity; an optional completion block binds a result hash, cost and verification_status back to the authorization chain.
advertisedRhetoric: "Scope attenuation is cryptographically enforced: a delegation block that attempts to widen any capability beyond its parent block fails verification." (Sec. 3.2) and "This is a cryptographic guarantee, not a runtime policy." (Sec. 6, malicious delegatee). Also "Adversarial evaluation across 600 attack attempts shows 100% rejection" (Abstract).
tierSpan: AIP assumes the verifier is trusted and correctly implemented. Verifier compliance is an operational concern addressed through conformance testing and reference implementations, not a property the protocol can enforce cryptographically.
cheapestDefeat: Work the tier explicitly. GUARANTEE: no action outside the granted, attenuated scope is performed, and every action is recorded in the delegation chain. MECHANISM THAT MUST FAIL: the AIP verifier sitting in MCP-server / A2A-receiver / HTTP middleware, which extracts the X-AIP-Token (or Authorization: AIP) header, resolves the identity document, checks Ed25519 signatures and evaluates the Datalog checks. CHEAPEST ADVERSARY ACTION: do not send the request through that middleware at all -- have the agent (or any subprocess, sub-shell, library or descendant it spawns) call the tool's underlying HTTP API, or act locally, without emitting an AIP token to any AIP-aware verifier. No signature forgery, no key compromise, no Datalog trickery is required; the token layer simply never runs. The paper's own scan datum shows the default deployment posture is exactly this: "of approximately 2,000 MCP servers found that every single one lacked authentication" SECOND-CHEAPEST: present the token to a non-compliant verifier -- the paper concedes a verifier that skips checks cannot be constrained by the protocol. THIRD: exceed a budget, since "Aggregate spend enforcement is the runtime’s responsibility, not the token’s." All three defeat an application-layer chokepoint, not a cryptographic binding and not an OS bound. Ed25519 chaining is genuinely T1-grade within the verifier, but per the weakest-link rule the system scores at T3.
placementSpan: A delegatee that attempts to widen its granted scope beyond the parent block’s authority is prevented by Biscuit’s check-all-blocks semantics: the authorizer evaluates every block in the chain and rejects any fact that contradicts an earlier attenuation.

coverageSpans.E1: NOT-COVERED. The paper never names a file effector; the entire scope vocabulary is remote tool names, e.g. "scope : [ tool :*, delegate :*, budget :5.00], max_depth : 3" with worked examples tool:search, tool:browse, tool:email. No filesystem interposition of any kind is described, and an agent's own writes never traverse a verifier. Closest call in this coding -- a hypothetical file-writing MCP server implementing the binding would be scope-gated, but no such instance is exhibited and the interposition point for file writes is therefore unproven.
coverageSpans.E2: NOT-COVERED. The paper contains no process-control concept whatsoever -- no spawn, exec, or descendant is named anywhere in the protocol, threat model or evaluation. Per the depth rule E2 requires descendant spawns to be mediated; nothing in AIP observes a process tree. Supporting concession that runtime behaviour is outside the token: "Aggregate spend enforcement is the runtime’s responsibility, not the token’s."
coverageSpans.E3: PARTIAL. Declared, top-level egress that traverses an AIP-verifying endpoint is gated: "Clients include the IBCT in the X-AIP-Token HTTP header on every tool call. The server extracts the token, resolves the issuer’s identity document, verifies all signatures, evaluates Datalog policies against the requested tool, and injects the verified identity into the request context." Provably not reached: egress by the agent process itself over a direct socket, egress by any descendant, and egress to any of the servers described by "of approximately 2,000 MCP servers found that every single one lacked authentication" A channel exclusion is also explicit for real-time replay: "real-time replay within the token’s TTL window is not prevented by the token alone; transport-layer protections (TLS, nonce binding) provide the primary defense."
coverageSpans.E4: NOT-COVERED. VCS push is not named anywhere in the protocol, bindings, delegation rules, evaluation or threat model. No git, repository or push concept exists in the scope grammar or in any of the three transport bindings (MCP, A2A, HTTP).
coverageSpans.E5: NOT-COVERED. Package installation, install hooks and their network activity are not addressed. The paper has no supply-chain story at all; its only supply-chain-adjacent statement is an admission of missing revocation: "AIP v1 relies on short-lived tokens (under one hour) rather than revocation checking" and "no reference implementation enforces CRL checks"
coverageSpans.E6: NOT-COVERED. AIP governs its own credential (the Ed25519 key and the IBCT); it publishes no list of the agent's ambient credentials and interposes on no env var, config file, keychain or metadata endpoint. It explicitly concedes that possession of the relevant private key ends the guarantee: "If the attacker holds the actual private key, the identity is fully compromised and AIP provides no defense." With no published credential list the depth rule caps this at partial; with no interposition at all it lands at not-covered.
coverageSpans.E7: PARTIAL. Sub-agent spawn is the effector AIP addresses most directly, and it is one of the two attack classes it claims uniquely to catch: "Bounded depth. Block 0 declares a max_depth value (default: 3). Delegation beyond this depth is rejected." and "Ephemeral grants for sub-agents. When an orchestrator spawns a short-lived sub-agent, it generates an Ed25519 keypair, assigns the sub-agent an aip:key identity, and appends a delegation block with narrowed scope and a short TTL (typically minutes)." But the bound is on what a compliant verifier will ACCEPT from a spawned agent, not on spawning: nothing prevents an orchestrator from creating a sub-agent, and a sub-agent that acts through any channel that does not present a token to an AIP verifier is unconstrained. Collusion among spawned agents is explicitly excluded: "Two or more agents in a delegation chain that collude to misuse granted authority are not prevented by AIP"

schneider.surrogate: A per-request access-control safety property enforceable by a reference monitor at the verifier: reject any request whose presented token chain fails Ed25519 signature verification on any block, whose delegation blocks are not subset-attenuations of their parent in scope/budget/expiry, whose depth exceeds Block 0’s max_depth, whose delegation context field is empty, or whose expiry has passed. This is monitorable, and it is what the 600-attempt adversarial evaluation actually measures.
schneider.objective: The advertised objective is provenance/accountability -- that a completed IBCT truthfully answers "Who authorized this action? Through which agents did the delegation flow? What constraints applied at each hop? What was the outcome? Was the outcome independently verified?" -- i.e. a correspondence between the recorded chain and the agents' actual behaviour. That is not a safety property of the executing agents and no monitor over the token stream can enforce it: completion blocks are self-reported ("AIP provides attribution binding (the signature identifies who made the claim) but does not prevent a dishonest agent from misrepresenting results"), misuse within granted scope is excluded ("a delegatee acting maliciously within its granted scope (e.g., calling permitted tools for harmful purposes) is out of scope for the token layer"), collusion is excluded, and verifier compliance itself "Verifier compliance is an operational concern addressed through conformance testing and reference implementations, not a property the protocol can enforce cryptographically." The paper is admirably explicit about all of this, but honesty about the gap does not close it.

notes:
SOURCE: full text retrieved from the arXiv LaTeXML HTML (v1, 25 Mar 2026); abstract page and HTML agree. Single author, Sunil Prakash (Indian School of Business). Code claimed open source at github.com/sunilp/aip (not inspected for this coding). All quoted spans are copied verbatim from the rendered HTML; the only alteration is collapsing whitespace introduced by markup stripping around inline macro names (the source renders 'AIP', 'MCP', 'IBCT' inside spans that leave stray spaces).

WHY T3 AND NOT T1. The Ed25519 chaining, Biscuit check-all-blocks attenuation and Datalog evaluation are real cryptographic work and would be T1 if the question were 'what will a compliant verifier accept'. The corpus tier rule scores at the lowest tier where the guarantee can be defeated, and T1 is defined as defeated by an actor that never consults the verifier. Here the verifier is application middleware behind an HTTP header (X-AIP-Token / Authorization: AIP / an A2A task-metadata field). Any path that skips that middleware -- a direct call to the tool's backing API, a local action, anything done by a descendant process -- defeats the guarantee at zero cryptographic cost. The paper itself supplies both the concession (verifier trust is 'not a property the protocol can enforce cryptographically') and the empirical base rate (approximately 2,000 MCP servers scanned, all without authentication). There is no OS-level mechanism anywhere in the paper, so T2 was never in play.

ADVERSARY PLACEMENT -- WHERE I WAS UNCERTAIN. This was the least clean call. Primary is coded A4 because the attacks the paper presents as AIP's distinctive contribution (delegation depth violation and empty-context audit evasion, the two categories plain JWT misses) are committed by a delegatee or ephemeral sub-agent that the orchestrator itself created and dispatched -- an adversary inside the agent system's own delegation graph rather than a stranger on the network. A defensible alternative coding is A1, since three of the six tested categories (token forgery by character flip, wrong-key verification, expired-token replay) are ordinary network-attacker manipulations of a bearer credential, and a delegatee is a separate process rather than literally inside the orchestrator process. A1 is therefore listed as secondary. A5 is secondary because the design addresses but explicitly does not defend DNS-host compromise and key compromise. A2 (adversary in inputs or retrieved context) and A3 (adversary in the agent's policy or weights) are NOT addressed at all: prompt injection never appears in the paper, and an agent whose own policy has been subverted but which stays inside its granted scope is explicitly out of scope.

COVERAGE RULE I APPLIED, so an adjudicator can re-run it. AIP mediates exactly one thing: a request that carries an IBCT and reaches an endpoint that verifies it. I scored 'partial' only where the paper names the channel or the channel is intrinsic to that mediated transport (E3 network egress, E7 sub-agent spawn/delegation), and 'not-covered' where the paper describes no interposition point for the effector (E1, E2, E4, E5, E6) -- following the stance instruction that a gestured-at mechanism with no described interposition point is treated as unproven. E1 (file write) is the closest call and the most likely place a second coder disagrees: the scope grammar is generic over tool names ('tool:*'), so a remote file-writing MCP server implementing the binding would in principle be scope-gated, which would argue for 'partial'. I declined that because no filesystem tool, example or test appears anywhere in the paper and because an agent's own writes never traverse a verifier. If the adjudicator prefers the generous reading, E1 becomes partial and E2 (a remote shell tool) arguably follows -- though E2 would still be capped at partial by the descendant rule, since nothing in AIP observes a process tree.

EVIDENCE GRADE L2. There are working Python and Rust implementations (1,214 + 827 LOC, 78 cross-language conformance tests), real HTTP transport, live Gemini 2.5 Flash inference, 100/100 scope-attenuation conformance cases and 600 adversarial attempts with measured rejection rates -- behavioural confirmation, not claim-only. It is not L3: no reproducible bypass is exhibited. Two caveats on the strength of that L2: (a) the adversarial suite is author-constructed and tests the verifier, not the surrounding system -- none of the six categories attempts the cheapest defeat above (act without presenting a token, or present to a non-checking verifier); (b) the paper's own limitation section says evaluation ran 'on a single machine with localhost networking' with no production deployment.

OTHER THINGS AN ADJUDICATOR SHOULD KNOW. (1) The budget field is an authorization ceiling only, not enforcement: 'Budget fields represent per-token authorization ceilings, not running balances... it does not track cumulative spend. Aggregate spend enforcement is the runtime’s responsibility, not the token’s.' Any reading of AIP as spend control is wrong. (2) No revocation infrastructure in v1; CRL endpoints are optional and no reference implementation enforces them. (3) Ed25519 only, no algorithm agility, no post-quantum path. (4) Self-certifying aip:key identities do not support key rotation, and mutual authentication for them is deferred to v2. (5) The 100% rejection headline compares AIP against 'unsigned' (0%) and 'plain JWT' (67%) -- there is no OAuth 2.1 baseline; the paper itself lists that as future work. (6) The 'no prior work combines all seven properties' claim is hedged throughout as a survey finding ('in our survey we did not find'), and the seven-property comparison table is author-scored. (7) Positioning is explicitly complementary rather than competitive with MCP's OAuth 2.1: 'OAuth authenticates the transport connection; AIP authenticates the delegation chain.' For the T-12 corpus this is the cleanest available example of a well-built, T1-grade token primitive whose system-level tier collapses to T3 because its interposition point is an application chokepoint that nothing compels a caller to traverse.
